	eval = run_vignette

library(lame)
```


## What the fast route gives

`ame()` and `lame()` fit AME models by MCMC. The package also fits the same
model

  z_ij = mu + beta'x_ij + a_i + b_j + u_i'v_j + e_ij

without sampling, in seconds:

- `ame_als()` for one network, or `ame(..., method = "als")`
- `lame_als()` for a panel, or `lame(..., method = "als")`
- `ame_als_bootstrap()` for bootstrap intervals

The fast fit is the empirical-Bayes estimate of the model the samplers draw
from. The sender and receiver effects and the latent positions keep the
samplers' Gaussian priors, the variance components are estimated from the
data, and every estimate comes with a standard error: the coefficients, the
variance components, the sender and receiver effects, and the latent positions
and product. The
result works with `coef()`, `confint()`, `summary()`, `fitted()`, `predict()`,
`simulate()`, `latent_positions()`, `ab_plot()`, `uv_plot()` and `gof_plot()`.

Use it to compare specifications and ranks, to fit large networks, and to
start a sampler at the answer.

## Agreement with the sampler on the shipped data

The table sets the fast fit beside the default `ame()` or `lame()` call on three
shipped data sets, each with two latent dimensions. The coefficient gap is the
largest difference between the two sets of coefficients, in posterior standard
deviations. The standard-error ratio divides the fast fit's standard errors by
those posterior standard deviations. The last column is the rank correlation
of the two sets of fitted values. Times are seconds on the same machine.

| Data | Fast fit | Sampler | Coefficient gap | SE ratio | Fitted correlation |
|------|---------:|--------:|----------------:|---------:|-------------------:|
| `IR90s` log exports, normal | 15.3 | 168.9 | 0.13 | 1.00 | 1.000 |
| `YX_bin_list`, binary panel | 1.6 | 720.9 | 0.07 | 1.03 | 1.000 |
| `comtrade`, normal panel with `dynamic_uv` | 15.8 | 254.4 | 0.23 | 0.88 | 0.989 |

On simulated data the picture is the same. Across 44 normal networks
(directed, symmetric and bipartite, ranks 0 to 3) the intercept was within 0.07
and the slopes within 0.09 posterior standard deviations of a long sampler run,
with standard errors 0.97 to 1.05 times the posterior standard deviations.
Across 1,000 simulated normal panels the 95 percent intervals of the dyadic
slope covered the generating value in 94.3 percent. `?ame_als` reports the
larger simulations.

## A first fit

```{r first-fit}
set.seed(1)
n <- 40
a <- rnorm(n, 0, 0.5); b <- rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
u <- rnorm(n, 0, 0.8); v <- rnorm(n, 0, 0.8) # a rank-one latent term
Xd <- matrix(rnorm(n * n), n, n)
Y <- 0.5 + 0.8 * Xd + outer(a, b, "+") + tcrossprod(u, v) + matrix(rnorm(n * n), n, n)
diag(Y) <- NA

fit <- ame_als(Y, Xdyad = Xd, R = 1, family = "normal", verbose = FALSE)
fit
```

The estimates and their 95 percent intervals, beside the values that generated
the data:

```{r first-fit-truth}
round(cbind(truth = c(0.5, 0.8), estimate = coef(fit), confint(fit)), 3)
round(fit$VC, 3)
```

`va` and `vb` are the variances of the sender and receiver effects (0.25 in the
simulation), `cab` their covariance, `rho` the dyadic correlation and `ve` the
noise variance (1 in the simulation).

## Sparse and dense binary networks

The density of a binary network is the share of its observed cells that are
ties, with the diagonal of a one-mode network left out and the periods of a
panel pooled. Outside densities of 0.2 to 0.8 the fast route pulls slopes
toward zero, biases the intercept and gives intervals that cover less often
than stated, so a fast fit there comes with a warning. For such networks the
sampler, `ame()` or `lame()`, is the better choice.

## Choosing the rank

Each fast fit reports `fit$eb$log_marginal`, the Laplace approximation to the
log marginal likelihood with the effects and the positions integrated out.
Unlike the deviance, it does not improve with every added dimension. The rank
with the largest value is the one the data support, and the difference between
two ranks is an approximate log Bayes factor. Fitting four ranks takes a few
seconds:

```{r rank}
ev <- sapply(
	0:3,
	function(r)
		ame_als(
			Y,
			Xdyad = Xd,
			R = r,
			family = "normal",
			verbose = FALSE
		)$eb$log_marginal
)
data.frame(R = 0:3, log_marginal = round(ev - ev[1], 1))
```

The data were generated with one latent dimension, and rank 1 has the largest
value. In simulation the largest value named the generating rank in every
normal network with at least 8 noise variances of signal per loading (252
networks).

A fit also measures how much the data say about its latent product
(`fit$eb$variational$information`). When that is too little to locate the
positions well at the rank requested, the fit reports the positions and the
product shrunken toward zero, with standard errors that carry the extra
uncertainty, and prints a note suggesting a smaller rank. Static and dynamic
fits do the same.

## Binary and count networks

Binary fits use the probit link and count fits the log link, so the
coefficients are on the same scale as those of `ame()` and `lame()`. A directed
fit models the dyadic correlation as the samplers do: the two cells of a dyad
are one bivariate observation and `fit$VC["rho"]` is their correlation.
`fitted()` and `predict()` return probabilities for binary data and mean counts
for count data.

A count is `Poisson(exp(z))`, with `z` the linear predictor plus normal noise
of variance `ve`, which the fit estimates. Because the actor effects have a
prior, an actor with no counts keeps a finite effect. In this network one actor
sends nothing and another receives nothing:

```{r poisson}
set.seed(4)
nc <- 30
xc <- matrix(rnorm(nc * nc), nc, nc)
ac <- rnorm(nc, 0, 0.7); bc <- rnorm(nc, 0, 0.7)
Yc <- matrix(
	rpois(
		nc * nc,
		exp(
			-0.3 + 0.5 * xc + outer(ac, bc, "+") +
				rnorm(nc * nc, 0, 0.6)
		)
	),
	nc,
	nc
)
# one actor sends no counts and another receives none
Yc[2, ] <- 0; Yc[, 5] <- 0
diag(Yc) <- NA
fc <- ame_als(Yc, Xdyad = xc, R = 0, family = "poisson", verbose = FALSE)
round(cbind(estimate = coef(fc), confint(fc)), 3)
round(c(ve = fc$VC[["ve"]], sender_2 = fc$a[[2]], receiver_5 = fc$b[[5]]), 2)
```

The slope was generated as 0.5 and the noise variance as 0.36. The two silent
actors get large negative effects, shrunk toward the rest of the network as in
the sampler.

A binary network of 80 actors with a density of 0.52, used in the next two
sections:

```{r binary}
set.seed(2)
nb <- 80
ab <- rnorm(nb, 0, 0.5); bb <- rnorm(nb, 0, 0.5)
Xb <- matrix(rnorm(nb * nb), nb, nb)
Yb <- 1 * (0.8 * Xb + outer(ab, bb, "+") + matrix(rnorm(nb * nb), nb, nb) > 0)
diag(Yb) <- NA
fb <- ame_als(Yb, Xdyad = Xb, R = 0, family = "binary", verbose = FALSE)
round(cbind(truth = c(0, 0.8), estimate = coef(fb), confint(fb)), 3)
```

## Uncertainty

`vcov()`, `confint()` and `summary()` of a fast fit use Laplace standard errors:
the inverse information of all the parameters at the fit, with the uncertainty
in the scale of the latent positions included. They cover every coefficient,
sender and receiver covariates included, and need no refitting. The same fit
carries standard errors for the variance components (`fit$VC_se`, shown by
`summary()`), the sender and receiver effects (`fit$a_sd`, `fit$b_sd`) and the
latent positions and product cells (`fit$U_sd`, `fit$V_sd`, `fit$UVPM_sd`, and
`posterior_sd` in `latent_positions()`).

`ame_als_bootstrap()` gives bootstrap intervals instead. It simulates networks
from the fitted model and refits each one; a quantity the replicates cannot
give an error for keeps its analytic one, and the summary names it:

```{r bootstrap}
bt <- ame_als_bootstrap(
	fb,
	R = 30,
	type = "parametric",
	seed = 1,
	verbose = FALSE
)
summary(bt)
```

Every replicate behind these intervals converged, and the summary says so. The
`ve` row is constant because the probit scale fixes the noise variance at 1.
Thirty replicates keep this example short; use 200 or more for intervals to
report. `bootstrap = N` in the fitting call does both steps at once, and
`type = "block"` resamples the periods of a panel of ten or more (a shorter
panel runs the parametric scheme, with a message). A dynamic fit keeps its own
standard errors, and `bootstrap = N` there leaves it with them.

## From a fast fit to a posterior

`als_start_vals()` turns a fast fit into starting values for the sampler, so
the chains begin where the fast fit ended:

```{r posterior}
fit_mcmc <- ame(
	Yb,
	Xdyad = Xb,
	family = "binary",
	R = 0,
	start_vals = als_start_vals(fb),
	burn = 200,
	nscan = 1000,
	odens = 5,
	verbose = FALSE,
	plot = FALSE,
	gof = FALSE,
	seed = 1
)

# estimates and 95 percent intervals from the three sources
terms <- names(coef(fb))
cmp <- rbind(
	data.frame(
		estimator = "Fast fit, Laplace",
		term = terms,
		estimate = unname(coef(fb)),
		lower = confint(fb)[terms, 1],
		upper = confint(fb)[terms, 2]
	),
	data.frame(
		estimator = "Fast fit, bootstrap",
		term = terms,
		estimate = unname(coef(fb)),
		lower = confint(bt)[terms, 1],
		upper = confint(bt)[terms, 2]
	),
	data.frame(
		estimator = "Sampler posterior",
		term = terms,
		estimate = unname(coef(fit_mcmc)[terms]),
		lower = confint(fit_mcmc)[terms, 1],
		upper = confint(fit_mcmc)[terms, 2]
	)
)
rownames(cmp) <- NULL
cbind(cmp[, 1:2], round(cmp[, 3:5], 3))
```

```{r posterior-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Coefficient plot for the binary network. The intercept and the dyadic slope each have three horizontal intervals, one for the Laplace interval of the fast fit, one for its bootstrap interval and one for the posterior interval of the sampler. Within each coefficient the three intervals nearly coincide."}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(
	cmp,
	aes(
		x = estimate,
		y = term,
		shape = estimator
	)
) +
	geom_pointrange(
		aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper),
		position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
		size = 0.5
	) +
	labs(
		x = "Coefficient (probit scale)",
		y = NULL,
		shape = NULL
	) +
	theme_bw() +
	theme(
		panel.border = element_blank(),
		axis.line = element_blank(),
		axis.ticks = element_blank(),
		legend.position = "top"
	)
```

The three intervals for each coefficient nearly coincide, and each contains the
value that generated the data (0 for the intercept, 0.8 for the slope).

## Panels and dynamic effects

`lame_als()` fits a panel with effects and positions shared across the periods,
as a `lame()` fit without dynamic options does. This is the second row of the
first table, a panel with a density of 0.51:

```{r panel}
data(YX_bin_list)
Yl <- lapply(YX_bin_list$Y, function(y) 1 * (y > 0))
lf <- lame_als(Yl, Xdyad = YX_bin_list$X, R = 2, family = "binary", verbose = FALSE)
round(cbind(estimate = coef(lf), confint(lf)), 3)
```

`lame(..., method = "als")` takes the dynamic options of the sampler:
`dynamic_ab` for sender and receiver effects that move over time,
`dynamic_beta` for coefficients that move, and `dynamic_uv` for positions that
move. The effects follow the AR(1) process of `lame()`. The fit sets its
persistence and innovation scale from the data as smoothing settings, kept on
the fit for prediction; the sampler estimates the persistence with an
interval. Here the sender and
receiver effects of 30 actors move over 8 periods with persistence 0.7 and
innovation scale 0.3:

```{r dynamic}
set.seed(7)
nn <- 30; Tn <- 8
nmn <- paste0("a", sprintf("%02d", 1:nn))
# an actor level plus an AR(1) deviation in each period
ar1_paths <- function() {
	level <- rnorm(nn, 0, 0.6)
	dev <- matrix(0, nn, Tn)
	dev[, 1] <- rnorm(nn, 0, 0.3 / sqrt(1 - 0.7^2))
	for (t in 2:Tn) dev[, t] <- 0.7 * dev[, t - 1] + rnorm(nn, 0, 0.3)
	level + dev
}
an <- ar1_paths(); bn <- ar1_paths()
xn <- lapply(
	seq_len(Tn),
	function(t)
		array(rnorm(nn * nn), c(nn, nn, 1), dimnames = list(nmn, nmn, "x"))
)
Yn <- lapply(seq_len(Tn), function(t) {
	m <- 0.3 + 0.7 * xn[[t]][, , 1] + outer(an[, t], bn[, t], "+") +
		matrix(rnorm(nn * nn, 0, 0.8), nn)
	diag(m) <- NA
	dimnames(m) <- list(nmn, nmn)
	m
})
fn <- lame(
	Yn,
	Xdyad = xn,
	family = "normal",
	method = "als",
	dynamic_ab = TRUE,
	verbose = FALSE
)
round(confint(fn)["x_dyad", ], 3)
round(c(ve = fn$VC[["ve"]]), 2)
# estimated sender and receiver paths against the generating ones
round(c(sender = cor(c(fn$a_dynamic), c(an)), receiver = cor(c(fn$b_dynamic), c(bn))), 3)
```

The interval of the slope contains 0.7, the noise variance is close to 0.64,
and the estimated paths follow
the generating ones. Binary and count panels take the same call, and a panel
whose actors enter and leave is aligned by actor name. On the shipped
`comtrade` panels (30 countries, 10 years) the 18 dynamic fits tried, with
moving effects and moving positions, took 9.5 to 23 seconds each.

## What each route covers

| | Fast route | Sampler |
|---|---|---|
| Families | normal, binary, poisson | normal, binary, poisson, ordinal, cbin, frn |
| Networks | directed, symmetric, bipartite | directed, symmetric, bipartite |
| Covariates | `Xdyad`, `Xrow`, `Xcol` | `Xdyad`, `Xrow`, `Xcol` |
| Binary density | any; a warning outside 0.2 to 0.8 | any |
| Latent rank | any `R`, compared by `fit$eb$log_marginal` | any `R` |
| Dynamic effects | `dynamic_ab`, `dynamic_beta`, `dynamic_uv` (`"ar1"`, `"t"`) | `dynamic_ab`, `dynamic_beta`, `dynamic_uv` (`"ar1"`, `"t"`, `"snap"`) |
| Uncertainty | Laplace standard errors for every estimate; optional bootstrap for static fits | posterior draws |
| Fit checks | `gof_plot()` by simulation from the fit | posterior predictive `gof_plot()`, `custom_gof`, `trace_plot()` |
| Methods | `coef`, `vcov`, `confint`, `summary`, `fitted`, `residuals`, `predict`, `simulate`, `latent_positions`, `ab_plot`, `uv_plot` | the same |

`ame(..., method = "als")` and `lame(..., method = "als")` take the call you
would give the sampler. Arguments that only a sampler uses, such as `nscan`,
`burn`, `odens` and `chains`, are named in a warning and ignored. `?ame_als`
and `?lame_als` document each estimator and the simulations behind the numbers
on this page.
